claim.citation: Thompson, D.W. (1917) On Growth and Form, Cambridge University Press, Ch. XVII 'On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms', pp. 770-773, Figs. 404-408
claim.text: The human skull, inscribed in Cartesian coordinates and deformed, gives the skulls of chimpanzee, baboon and dog: ape/human skull difference is a whole-diagram transformation (notably of the facial/cranial proportions).

sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C1_whole_diagram: p. 771: corresponding points in the chimpanzee's skull 'may be at once linked up by smoothly curved lines of intersection, which form a new system of co-ordinates and constitute a simple projection of our human skull' (Figs. 404-406).
sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C2_same_order_baboon: p. 771: for the baboon (Fig. 407) 'the transformation is of precisely the same order, and differs only in an increased intensity or degree of deformation'.
sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C3_logarithmic_area_gradient: p. 771: 'as we pass from above downwards and from behind forwards, the corresponding areas of the network are seen to increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order in the lower as compared with the higher type of skull'.
sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C4_chimp_nearer_than_baboon: p. 772: 'the chimpanzee's skull is much nearer to the human type than is the baboon's'; the series is 'not, strictly speaking, continuous'.
sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C5_dog_different_lines: p. 773: dog (Fig. 408) 'tapers away in front, a triangular taking the place of a rectangular conformation', 'progressive elongation, or pulling out, of the whole forepart', vertical ordinates 'become curved, with their convexity directed forwards'; the ape network 'is by no means intermediate' between man and dog.
sub_claims_extracted_from_source_text.C6_facial_cranial_proportions: p. 770: 'the main differences between the human and the simian types depend upon the enlargement or expansion of the brain and braincase in man, and the relative diminution or enfeeblement of his jaws'; 'the facial angle increases from an oblique angle to nearly a right angle in man'.

named_dataset.why_mismatch: The dataset is 3D cranial landmark data for 49 platyrrhine (New World monkey) species. Thompson's Figs. 404-408 claim concerns Homo sapiens, Pan troglodytes, a baboon (Papio) and the domestic dog (Canis familiaris) in 2D lateral profile. None of the claim's four taxa occurs in a platyrrhine-only dataset, so it cannot test the claim and is NOT used for the verdict (per the T1917 override, it is not fitted as an analogue).

A_thompson_1917_figures.leaf_to_page_rule: printed page = leaf - 20 (leaf 789 = p. 770, leaf 790 = p. 771, leaf 792 = p. 773)
A_thompson_1917_figures.species_match: EXACT - Homo sapiens, Pan troglodytes ('chimpanzee'), baboon, dog: the four taxa named in the claim
A_thompson_1917_figures.limitation: These are Thompson's drawings. Fig. 405's chimpanzee net is drawn without the skull and was digitised node-by-node (30 nodes, skeleton-junction detection + manual corners). The baboon (Fig. 407) and dog (Fig. 408) nets are drawn over heavy skull outlines and could not be extracted reliably by the same automatic method; those two taxa are tested on real specimens (dataset B) only.
